findings.finding: Insights: Scores are binary (wins give 2^{20‑i}); equal‑score pairing forces a perfect binary tournament → final scores are a permutation of 0…2^{20}‑1. Any permutation respecting the “bitwise‑lexicographic” order (higher bits decided earlier) is attainable. Count = product_{i=0}^{19} (2^{i}!)^{2^{20‑i‑1}}. Compute v₂, v₅ of this product; k = min(v₂,v₅) mod 10⁵. Pitfalls: ensure pairing constraint yields exactly that count; avoid double‑counting.

Insights: Final scores are binary strings of length 20; each round decides one bit among runners with equal prefix. Pairings can be any perfect matching within each score‑group. The process yields exactly the linear extensions of the poset formed by the 20‑level binary tree where each node’s two children are comparable only after their parent’s bit is set. Thus N equals the number of ways to label the 2²⁰ leaves with distinct speeds consistent with this tree‑order, i.e. the number of linear extensions of a complete binary tree of height 20. Compute N = ∏_{k=1}^{2^{20}} (size of subtree containing leaf k)⁻¹? (Pitfall: mis‑counting matchings; need exact formula for extensions of a full binary tree.)

Insights: After i rounds each i‑bit binary score appears 2^{20‑i} times. In round i, winners must be the faster half of each equal‑score group; otherwise no pairing can give all winners faster than their opponents. Thus each round forces the top half of each group to get a 1‑bit. Consequently the final ranking is uniquely determined: the fastest runner gets 111…1, next fastest 111…0, etc. Hence N=1, k=0, answer 0.

Insights: After i rounds each i‑bit binary score appears 2^{20‑i} times. Final scores are a permutation of 0…2^{20}‑1. A runner’s binary string must be lexicographically ≥ any slower runner’s (first differing bit 1 for faster). Thus feasible rankings = linear extensions of the poset where x<y iff binary(x) < binary(y) in lexicographic order. Count = number of permutations respecting this total order = (2^{20})! / ∏_{b} (size of subtree at b). Compute exponent of 10 in N, then k mod 10^5. Pitfalls: ensure correct poset (lexicographic), handle huge factorial via Legendre for 2,5.

Number of possible rankings = Π_{i=1}^{20} (C(2^{21‑i},2^{20‑i}))^{2^{i‑1}}. For m≥1, v₂(C(2^m,2^{m‑1}))=1; v₅(C(2^m,2^{m‑1})) from Legendre: v₅((2^m)!)-2v₅((2^{m‑1})!). Compute v₂(N)=Σ2^{i‑1}=2^{20}‑1. Compute v₅(N)=Σ2^{i‑1}·v₅(C(...)). Sum gives k=min(v₂,v₅). Return k mod 100000. Pitfall: ensure v₅(C) correctly evaluated; use v₅(n!)= (n‑s₅(n))/(5‑1).

Insights: Final scores are distinct 20‑bit strings; ordering = sorting these binary numbers. Each round splits every equal‑score group (size 2m) into winners/losers of size m obeying “ballot” (Dyck) condition → Catalan Cₘ possibilities. Thus any permutation achievable iff its binary‑tree labeling respects these Catalan splits. Count = product over all groups of C_{size/2}. Compute N = ∏_{r=0}^{19} C_{2^{r}}^{2^{20‑r‑1}}. Find largest k with 10^k|N; output k mod 10⁵. Pitfalls: ensure groups are independent, use exact Catalan numbers, handle huge exponents via prime‑factorization (2,5).

Insights: Final scores are unique 20‑bit win strings. At round i, each score class (same prefix) splits into winners/losers of size half. A subset can be winners iff every winner has a slower opponent → the winners must be a “dominant” set: after sorting speeds, for any prefix the #winners ≤ #players‑#winners (i.e., no winner is among the k slowest). This yields a bijection between possible final rankings and linear extensions of the poset where i ≺ j if i must rank above j (i faster than j) whenever i cannot be paired to lose to j. Counting these extensions gives N. Pitfall: assuming any half‑subset works; need Hall’s condition → dominant sets only.

Insights: Final rankings = recursive splits of size‑2ⁿ groups; each split’s winner set must be a Catalan‑valid dominant subset → C_{size/2} choices. Hence N = F(2²⁰) with F(2^k)=C_{2^{k‑1}}·F(2^{k‑1})². So  

N = ∏_{i=0}^{19} C_{2^{i}}^{2^{19‑i}}.  

Compute v₂(N), v₅(N) via vₚ(C_m)=vₚ((2m)!)-2vₚ(m!)-vₚ(m+1). Sum over i with multiplicities 2^{19‑i}. k = min(v₂,v₅). Return k mod 100 000.

Insights: tournament splits each equal‑size group into winners/losers → recursion f(2^i)=C_{2^{i‑1}}·f(2^{i‑1})². Hence N=∏_{j=0}^{19}C_{2^{j}}^{2^{19‑j}}.  

Valuations: v₂(C_{2^j})=1 for j≥1, 0 for j=0 ⇒ v₂(N)=∑_{j=1}^{19}2^{19‑j}=2^{19}‑1=524 287.  

Compute v₅(C_{2^j}) via Legendre: v₅(C_n)=v₅((2n)!)-v₅(n!)-v₅((n+1)!). Sum weighted: v₅(N)=∑_{j=0}^{19}2^{19‑j}·v₅(C_{2^{j}})=121 818.  

k=min(v₂,v₅)=121 818. Answer k mod 10⁵ = 21 818.  

Pitfalls: assume order‑preserving; actually any split obeying “winners never exceed losers in any prefix” → Catalan count. Use Catalan oddness rule (odd iff n=2^k‑1) → v₂=1 for powers of two >1. Use exact v₅ via factorial valuations.

Insights: After 20 rounds each runner gets a unique 20‑bit score (wins=1). In round i, within any equal‑prefix group we may choose any subset of half the players as winners **iff** there exists a perfect matching where each winner is paired with a slower opponent. By Hall’s theorem this is equivalent to the “ballot” condition: scanning the group from fastest to slowest, at any prefix the number of chosen winners never exceeds the number of remaining players. Such subsets are counted by Catalan numbers Cₘ = (1/(m+1))·(2m choose m) for a group of size 2m.  

Thus each round independently contributes a product of Catalan numbers over all groups formed. After 20 rounds the groups are all size 2, giving C₁=1 each, so the total number of possible final orderings N equals the product of Catalan numbers for all intermediate groups. Compute  

\[
N=\prod_{i=1}^{20}\;C_{2^{20-i}}^{\,2^{i-1}}
\]

(where there are \(2^{i-1}\) groups of size \(2^{20-i+1}=2\cdot2^{20-i}\) in round i).  

Factor N, find the exponent \(k\) of 10 (i.e. min(v₂(N),v₅(N))). Use Legendre’s formula on each Catalan factor:  

\(C_n=\frac{(2n)!}{(n+1)!\,n!}\).  

Sum the 2‑adic and 5‑adic valuations over all factors, then \(k=\min(v_2(N),v_5(N))\). Finally output \(k\bmod 10^5\).  

Pitfalls: assume winners must be top half (false); must use Hall’s condition → Catalan count. Ensure correct exponents for each round’s group count. Use big‑integer arithmetic or valuation formulas; N itself is astronomically large.

Insights: Final scores are binary strings; tournament builds a full binary tree. Each internal node of size 2m can split winners (size m) in any Catalan‑allowed subset (Cₘ ways). Choices at nodes are independent.  

Result:  
\(N=\prod_{t=0}^{n-1}C_{2^{t}}^{\,2^{\,n-1-t}}\) for \(n=20\).  

Compute \(v_5(N)=\sum_{t=0}^{19}2^{19-t}\,v_5(C_{2^{t}})=121\,818\).  
\(v_2(N)=524\,287\).  

Thus \(k=\min(v_2,v_5)=121\,818\); \(k\bmod10^5=21\,818\).  

Pitfalls: forgetting the denominator \((m+1)\) in Catalan valuation; assuming all pairings give same ranking.

Insights: After 20 rounds each runner gets a unique 20‑bit score. In a group of 2n runners the possible winner‑sets (size n) are exactly the Catalan number Cₙ (Dyck‑path condition).  
Thus  

\[
N=\prod_{m=1}^{20}\Bigl(C_{2^{\,m-1}}\Bigr)^{2^{20-m}},\qquad 
C_{2^{m-1}}=\frac{\binom{2^{m}}{2^{m-1}}}{2^{m-1}+1}.
\]

For a prime p, \(v_p(N)=\sum_{m=1}^{20}2^{20-m}\bigl(v_p\!\bigl(\binom{2^{m}}{2^{m-1}}\bigr)-v_p(2^{m-1}+1)\bigr)\).

Using Legendre’s formula \(v_5\bigl(\binom{2^{m}}{2^{m-1}}\bigr)=\frac{2s_5(2^{m-1})-s_5(2^{m})}{4}\) (with \(s_5\) digit‑sum in base 5) gives  

\(a_m=v_5\bigl(\binom{2^{m}}{2^{m-1}}\bigr)=[0,0,1,1,1,0,3,1,0,1,3,3,3,4,1,2,3,5,5,6]\).

Subtract \(v_5(2^{m-1}+1)\) to get \(b_m\):  

\([0,0,0,1,1,0,2,1,0,1,1,3,3,4,0,2,3,5,4,6]\).

Then  

\[
v_5(N)=\sum_{m=1}^{20}2^{20-m}b_m=121\,818.
\]

\(v_2(N)=2^{20}-1=1\,048\,575\), so \(k=\min(v_2,v_5)=121\,818\).

Remainder of \(k\) mod \(10^5\) is **21 818**. 

Pitfalls: use Catalan (not central binomial) counts; ensure subtraction of \(v_5(2^{m-1}+1)\); verify with small cases (n=4,8).

Insights: Final scores are 20‑bit strings; each round splits a group of size 2k into winners/losers whose 0‑1 pattern (sorted by speed) must be a Dyck word ⇒ Cₖ choices.  
Total outcomes N = ∏_{j=0}^{19} C_{2^{j}}^{2^{19‑j}}.  
k = v₅(N)=∑_{j=0}^{19}2^{19‑j}·v₅(C_{2^{j}}).  
Use v₅(C_n)=v₅((2n)!)-2v₅(n!)-v₅(n+1). Compute for n=2^{j} (j≤19).  
Result: k=121 818 ⇒ k mod 10⁵ = **21 818**.  

Pitfalls: assume winners are top half (false); must count Dyck words. Verify v₂(N)>v₅(N) so 10‑valuation = v₅.
